title: ORA-01403 No Data Found in Oracle: Causes and Fixes
description: Fix ORA-01403 no data found in Oracle PL/SQL: handle NO_DATA_FOUND, avoid it with BULK COLLECT or cursors, and solve the 'data exists' cases.

reviewNotes: Examples written from the 19c docs and not executed; all need a test run (SQL*Plus or SQL Developer with SERVEROUTPUT ON). Please verify: (1) ORA-06512 line numbers in each error output (anonymous blocks at line 4/5/7; GET_SALARY line 12; GET_DEPT_NAME line 6) and replace schema name APP; (2) the function-in-SQL behaviour (NO_DATA_FOUND becomes NULL) is from MOS Doc 285496.1 whose body I could not read, plus community sources; (3) that RAISE_APPLICATION_ERROR from GET_SALARY does propagate when called via SELECT ... FROM dual; (4) the associative-array NO_DATA_FOUND description is confirmed in the 11g predefined exceptions table, not in the 19c page text I fetched. Overlap check: the published 'Top 10 common Oracle errors' post has a short ORA-01403 section; this is a dedicated deep guide and links to it.

data.text: ORA-01403: no data found means a SELECT ... INTO statement in PL/SQL returned zero rows. SELECT INTO must put exactly one row into its variables. When the WHERE clause matches nothing, PL/SQL raises the predefined exception NO_DATA_FOUND and, if nothing handles it, your block stops with ORA-01403.

The fix is almost never to hide the error. You decide what "no row" means for your code: a default value, a clear business error, or simply skipping the record. Then you write that decision into an exception handler or use a statement that does not raise the error. This guide shows each option with runnable examples, and explains the confusing case where you get ORA-01403 even though the data seems to exist.
What ORA-01403 means and when Oracle raises it

NO_DATA_FOUND is one of the predefined exceptions that PL/SQL declares in package STANDARD. Its SQLCODE is +100, not a negative number like most errors. You will usually see it together with ORA-06512, which tells you the line where it happened.

The most common source is SELECT INTO. The Oracle docs say it directly: if the SELECT INTO statement returns no rows, PL/SQL raises NO_DATA_FOUND. If it returns more than one row you get a different error, ORA-01422 (TOO_MANY_ROWS).
Many statements that look similar do not raise it. Knowing which is which removes most of the confusion:

content: Reading a missing element of an associative array
SELECT COUNT(*) or MAX(...) INTO variable
No error. The collection is empty (COUNT = 0)
UPDATE or DELETE that matches no rows
PL/SQL function called from a SQL query
No error. The function result is NULL

data.text: The last row surprises a lot of developers. It is covered in its own section below.
Sample setup

Create two small tables. Note two details on purpose: emp_code is a CHAR column, and one hire date has a time part. Both are used later to explain the "data exists but ORA-01403" case. Employee 104 points to department 40, which does not exist.

data.caption: Sample tables used in every example

data.text: Reproduce the error
This anonymous block looks up employee 999, who does not exist:

data.caption: SELECT INTO with no matching row

data.code:
ERROR at line 1:
ORA-01403: no data found
ORA-06512: at line 4
data.caption: Output (expected output)

data.text: Read the stack from the bottom. ORA-06512: at line 4 points at the SELECT (line 1 is DECLARE). The PUT_LINE never ran, because the exception jumped straight out of the block. In Oracle Database 23ai the message may also include a help link, but the codes are the same.
Fix 1: handle NO_DATA_FOUND with a default value

If a missing row is normal for your logic, catch the exception right where the query runs and set a sensible value. Wrap the query in its own small BEGIN ... END block so the rest of the code continues.

data.caption: Inner block with a local handler

data.code:
Name: Unknown

PL/SQL procedure successfully completed.
data.caption: Output (expected output)

data.text: The inner block keeps the handler close to the statement it protects. If you put the handler at the end of a long procedure instead, you cannot tell which of several queries failed, and the remaining work after the failed query is skipped.
Skip missing rows inside a loop
The same pattern lets a loop carry on past bad IDs. Here SYS.ODCINUMBERLIST, a number collection type supplied by Oracle, holds the IDs to process:

data.caption: Process every ID even when one is missing

data.code:
101: Asha Rao
999: not found, skipped
103: Meena Iyer

PL/SQL procedure successfully completed.
data.caption: Output (expected output)

data.title: Process many rows? Use one query
data.text: Running one SELECT INTO per ID is fine for a handful of values. For thousands, join the ID list to the table in a single query or use BULK COLLECT. You avoid the error and many round trips between PL/SQL and SQL.
Fix 2: raise a clear business error instead

Sometimes a missing row really is a problem, for example when a caller passes an employee ID that should exist. Do not swallow it. Convert the vague ORA-01403 into a message that tells the caller what went wrong, with RAISE_APPLICATION_ERROR.

data.caption: Translate ORA-01403 into a meaningful error

data.code:
ORA-20010: Employee 999 not found
ORA-06512: at "APP.GET_SALARY", line 12
data.caption: Output (expected output)

data.text: The caller now gets an error code in the -20000 to -20999 range reserved for applications, and a message with the actual ID. Your schema name will appear instead of APP. As the next sections show, this also matters when the function is called from SQL.
Fix 3: use a statement that does not raise the error
Option A: an aggregate function
An aggregate such as MAX or COUNT always returns exactly one row, even when no rows match. The Oracle docs suggest COUNT(*) for this reason.

data.caption: MAX returns NULL instead of raising

data.code:
Name: Unknown

PL/SQL procedure successfully completed.
data.caption: Output (expected output)

data.title: MAX also hides duplicates
data.text: If the WHERE clause matches two rows, MAX quietly picks one of them instead of raising ORA-01422. Use this trick only when the filter is on a primary key or unique column, where more than one row is impossible.
Option B: an explicit cursor and %NOTFOUND
A FETCH from an explicit cursor never raises ORA-01403. It sets %NOTFOUND to TRUE instead, and you test it with a normal IF.

data.caption: FETCH sets %NOTFOUND instead of raising

data.code:
No employee with that ID

PL/SQL procedure successfully completed.
data.caption: Output (expected output)

data.text: This is more code than SELECT INTO with a handler, and it does not complain if more than one row matches. Prefer it when you really want "the first row, if any" logic.
Option C: BULK COLLECT for zero or more rows

If the query can legitimately return zero, one or many rows, fetch into a collection. The docs state that PL/SQL does not raise an exception when a BULK COLLECT statement returns no rows, so you must check the collection yourself.

data.caption: An empty result is just COUNT = 0

data.code:
Rows found: 0

PL/SQL procedure successfully completed.
data.caption: Output (expected output)

data.text: ORA-01403 no data found but data exists
This is the most searched version of the problem. You run the query in SQL Developer or SQL*Plus, it returns a row, yet the PL/SQL code fails. Work through these causes in order.
1. The row is not committed, or you are in a different session

Other sessions cannot see rows you inserted until you commit. If you inserted test data in one SQL Developer tab and run the procedure from another connection or a job, the procedure sees nothing. Commit, then retry.
2. You are connected to a different schema or database

The same table name can exist in more than one schema, and in a multitenant setup in more than one pluggable database. The procedure runs with its owner's tables by default (definer's rights), not necessarily the ones you checked. Confirm where you are:

data.code:
SELECT USER,
       SYS_CONTEXT('USERENV', 'CURRENT_SCHEMA') AS current_schema,
       SYS_CONTEXT('USERENV', 'CON_NAME')       AS container
  FROM dual;
data.caption: Check user, schema and container

data.text: 3. A CHAR column compared with a VARCHAR2 variable

This one is subtle. emp_code is CHAR(6), so Oracle stores 'E101' padded with two trailing spaces. In plain SQL, WHERE emp_code = 'E101' finds the row, because both sides are CHAR or a text literal and Oracle uses blank-padded comparison. In PL/SQL you often compare with a VARCHAR2 variable, and then Oracle uses nonpadded comparison, so 'E101 ' is not equal to 'E101'.

data.caption: Works in SQL, fails in PL/SQL

data.code:
ERROR at line 1:
ORA-01403: no data found
ORA-06512: at line 5
data.caption: Output (expected output)

data.text: Fix it by declaring the variable with the column type, l_code employees.emp_code%TYPE. The value is then padded to six characters and the comparison matches. Avoid wrapping the column in RTRIM, because a function on the column stops Oracle from using a normal index on it. For new tables, use VARCHAR2 rather than CHAR.
4. A DATE column with a time part

Oracle DATE always stores a time. John's hire date is 15 January 2024 at 09:30, so WHERE hire_date = DATE '2024-01-15' matches nothing, because that literal means midnight. Your tool may only display the date part, which hides the difference.

data.code:
SELECT emp_name
  FROM employees
 WHERE hire_date >= DATE '2024-01-15'
   AND hire_date <  DATE '2024-01-16';
data.caption: Search a whole day with a range

data.code:
EMP_NAME
-----------
John Mathew
data.caption: Output (expected output)

data.text: The range finds every time on that day and can still use an index on hire_date. TRUNC(hire_date) = DATE ... also works, but it needs a function-based index to be fast.
5. The error came from a different statement

The failing query may not be the one you tested. Look at every ORA-06512 line in the stack. The top one is where the exception was raised, for example inside a function called by your procedure. In your own error logging, call DBMS_UTILITY.FORMAT_ERROR_BACKTRACE inside the handler so you keep that line number.
6. Case, spaces or a bind value you did not expect

'asha rao' does not equal 'Asha Rao', and a value read from a screen may carry a trailing space. Print the exact value you query with, for example DBMS_OUTPUT.PUT_LINE('[' || l_code || ']'), so hidden spaces show up between the brackets.
Why a function in a SELECT returns NULL instead of ORA-01403
Here is a function with no exception handler. It looks up a department name:

data.caption: A lookup function called from SQL

data.text: John's department 40 does not exist, so the function raised NO_DATA_FOUND. The query did not fail. The SQL engine treats NO_DATA_FOUND from a function like an empty result and returns NULL for that row. Oracle Support documents this behaviour (Doc ID 285496.1). Call the same function from PL/SQL and you get the error:

data.caption: Same function, called from PL/SQL

data.code:
ERROR at line 1:
ORA-01403: no data found
ORA-06512: at "APP.GET_DEPT_NAME", line 6
ORA-06512: at line 4
data.caption: Output (expected output)

data.text: So the same function behaves differently depending on who calls it. Make the behaviour explicit inside the function: return a default on purpose, or raise an application error as in Fix 2, which does reach the SQL caller. For reports like this one, an outer join is usually the better choice anyway, because SQL does the lookup in one pass instead of running a query per row:

data.code:
SELECT e.emp_name, d.dept_name
  FROM employees e
  LEFT JOIN departments d ON d.dept_id = e.dept_id
 ORDER BY e.emp_id;
data.caption: Outer join instead of a lookup function

data.text: ORA-01403 from an associative array
Reading an associative array (INDEX BY table) element that was never assigned also raises NO_DATA_FOUND. There is no SELECT anywhere, which makes this one hard to spot.

data.caption: Key 40 was never assigned

data.code:
ERROR at line 1:
ORA-01403: no data found
ORA-06512: at line 7
data.caption: Output (expected output)

data.text: Check the key with the EXISTS method before reading it: IF l_depts.EXISTS(40) THEN ... ELSE ... END IF;. EXISTS returns FALSE for a missing key instead of raising an error.
Common mistakes

items.content: WHEN OTHERS THEN NULL. It hides ORA-01403 and every other error, including real bugs. Catch NO_DATA_FOUND by name and handle only that.
Testing SQL%NOTFOUND after SELECT INTO. The exception is raised before your IF runs, so the check never helps. Use a handler, or a cursor FETCH where %NOTFOUND does work.
Running COUNT(*) first, then SELECT INTO. Two queries do the work of one, and another session can delete the row between them. One SELECT INTO with a handler is simpler and correct.
Expecting UPDATE or DELETE to raise ORA-01403. They never do. Check SQL%ROWCOUNT = 0 right after the statement if "no rows changed" is an error for you.
One handler at the bottom of a long procedure. You lose track of which query failed, and all the work after it is skipped. Put small handlers around the queries that can legitimately find nothing.
Returning NULL silently from lookup functions. Callers cannot tell "not found" from "value is NULL". Document the contract, or raise a clear error.

data.text: Best practices

items.content: Decide per query whether "no row" is normal (use a default) or a bug (raise an application error). Write that decision down in the handler.
Use %TYPE for variables you compare with columns. It prevents the CHAR versus VARCHAR2 trap and keeps lengths in sync.
Make sure the column in a single-row lookup is indexed, ideally a primary key or unique key. Then SELECT INTO is a fast index lookup, and duplicates cannot cause ORA-01422.
Log DBMS_UTILITY.FORMAT_ERROR_BACKTRACE when you re-raise, so the original line number is not lost.
Prefer joins over row-by-row lookup functions in queries. They are faster and do not hide errors.

data.text: Frequently asked questions
What is ORA-01403 no data found in Oracle?

It is the error behind the predefined PL/SQL exception NO_DATA_FOUND (SQLCODE +100). It is raised when SELECT INTO or EXECUTE IMMEDIATE ... INTO returns no rows, or when code reads an associative array element that does not exist.
How do I handle the no data found exception in Oracle?

Add EXCEPTION WHEN NO_DATA_FOUND THEN ... to the block that contains the query, ideally a small inner block around just that query. In the handler, assign a default, skip the record, or call RAISE_APPLICATION_ERROR with a clear message.
What does ORA-01403 with ORA-06512 mean?

ORA-01403 is the actual error. ORA-06512 lines are the call stack: each one names the program unit and line number the error passed through. The first ORA-06512 after ORA-01403 shows where the failing statement is.
Does BULK COLLECT raise NO_DATA_FOUND?
No. A BULK COLLECT that returns no rows leaves the collection empty and raises nothing. Check collection.COUNT = 0 yourself.
Why do I get ORA-01403 when the data exists?

The usual causes are uncommitted data, a different schema or container, a CHAR column compared with a VARCHAR2 variable, a DATE with a time part, or the error coming from a different query than the one you tested. Check the ORA-06512 line first.
Summary

items.content: ORA-01403 means SELECT INTO found no row, or a missing associative array key was read.
Read the first ORA-06512 line to find the failing statement.
Handle NO_DATA_FOUND by name in a small inner block, never with WHEN OTHERS THEN NULL.
Use a default when a missing row is normal, and RAISE_APPLICATION_ERROR when it is a bug.
Use BULK COLLECT or a cursor when zero or many rows are valid results.
For "data exists" cases, check commits, schema, CHAR vs VARCHAR2 and time parts of dates.
Remember that functions called from SQL turn NO_DATA_FOUND into NULL.

linkedin.post:
SELECT INTO found no row, your procedure died with ORA-01403, and the same query works fine in SQL Developer. Here is why.

ORA-01403 is NO_DATA_FOUND. SELECT INTO must return exactly one row. Zero rows raises it.

What actually fixes it:
→ Wrap the query in a small inner BEGIN ... EXCEPTION WHEN NO_DATA_FOUND block and set a default. Never use WHEN OTHERS THEN NULL.
→ If a missing row is a bug, convert it: RAISE_APPLICATION_ERROR(-20010, 'Employee not found').
→ BULK COLLECT, cursor FETCH, MAX() and UPDATE never raise ORA-01403. Check COUNT, %NOTFOUND or SQL%ROWCOUNT instead.
→ "But the data exists": a CHAR column compared with a VARCHAR2 variable does not match because of trailing spaces. Declare the variable with %TYPE.
→ A function called inside a SELECT that hits NO_DATA_FOUND returns NULL instead of failing. Same function from PL/SQL raises the error.

Which of these has bitten you in a real project: the CHAR padding, the DATE time part, or the silent NULL from a function?
